newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Trade ministers strive to clinch infotech deal.
newsitem.headline: Trade ministers strive to clinch infotech deal.

text.p: Trade ministers hunkered down on Thursday to try to clinch a deal to scrap tariffs in the lucrative global information technology sector before the close of this week's gathering of the World Trade Organisation.

The Big Four trade powers -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- have targetted the proposed pact to eliminate tariffs in the $600 billion infotech sector by the year 2000 as a key to declaring the WTO first ministerial meeting a real success.

The United States, whose high-tech firms would likely profit most from an Information Technology Agreement (ITA), has taken the lead in the push to forge a pact. Japan, also a huge player in the fast-growing sector, has backed the drive strongly.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Thursday expressed concern about whether the European Union wanted to complete a deal to liberalise trade in information technology by the conclusion of this week's WTO meeting.
Barshefsky told reporters following a speech to the American Chamber of Commerce here that "it is not at this point clear to me whether the European Union will move forward or not."
"The outcome of the European Council deliberations will tell the story of the EU's commitment to the ITA and thus its commitment to further trade liberalisation," Barshefsky said.

Barshefsky and the European Trade Commission Sir Leon Brittan met early on Thursday morning as the two sides continued an intense effort to resolve their differences on an information technology agreement that would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of computer and telecommunications products by 2000.
A European official described Barshefsky's comments as unfortunate. "No one's dragging their feet. They're just trying to work out the delicate issue of timing," the official said.
Trade ministers from the 15 EU states were being briefed by Brittan on Thursday morning about the progress of the talks.
A Japanese trade official said late on Wednesday that days of intense negotiations among the Big Four had narrowed gaps over the thorny problem of what products to include in the deal.
But one of Big Four partners, whom he did not identify, was still seeking to link an infotech deal with another issue, a position the official said Japan rejected.
"Among those (Big Four) members who want to get an agreement confined to the ITA alone, we are getting very close to agreement on product coverage," the official told reporters.
The Japanese official said Tokyo had offered to put on the table its own sensitive products "under certain conditions."

The EU has endorsed the drive to forge the infotech deal, but is taking a tough stance at the negotiating table, seeking to win compensation for scrapping its own info-tech tariffs, which are the highest among the Big Four.

Brittan earlier in the week suggested that an infotech deal be linked to a WTO drive to open up the global telecommunications sector. Telecommunications talks are set to resume formally in Geneva next month in an effort to meet a February 15 deadline.
The Big Four trade partners are meanwhile also seeking to bring on board as many other WTO members as possible, and are particularly keen to see key Asian economies sign on.
Some Asian members have already indicated support for the deal, but want flexibility over the timing of the tariff cuts.
Japanese officials have said a basic framework for the ITA agreed by the Big Four earlier in the week called for tariff cuts to begin from 1997 and be completed by the year 2000.
"There are two days left, and one can draw various scenarios for the outcome," the Japanese official said.
